title: What If the Statue of Liberty Walked Home?
central_question: If the Statue of Liberty finished the step she has been taking since 1886 and walked home to Paris, what would she pass, and who would notice?
setting: The Statue of Liberty finishes her step and walks from New York to Paris: Liberty Island at night, 1884 Paris, New York Harbor, the Atlantic floor, the Titanic, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Mont-Saint-Michel, the Arc de Triomphe, the Eiffel Tower and her little sister on the Île aux Cygnes.
fiction_notice: A cartoon thought experiment: statues cannot walk. Dee and Tony are fictional. The facts about the statue, the places and the sea are real and sourced; her walking speed and the pressure figure are our own arithmetic and labelled as such.

lines.text: Look closely at the Statue of Liberty's feet.
Her right heel is off the ground. She isn't standing still. She's mid-stride.
She has been since 1886. So what if, one night, she finished the step?
Ma'am? Ma'am, you can't... Okay.

badges.text: Her right heel is raised; broken chains lie at her feet (NPS)
A cartoon: statues can't walk. Dee and Tony are fictional

cards.title: What If the Statue of Liberty Walked Home?

lines.text: Home is Paris. She was built there, from copper sheets about as thick as two pennies.
In 1884 she stood finished above the Paris rooftops.
Then she was taken apart, packed into 214 crates, and shipped to New York.
Her iron skeleton was engineered by Gustave Eiffel.
A few years later, he built something taller.

badges.text: Copper skin 3/32 inch (2.4 mm): two pennies thick (NPS)
Assembled in Paris 1881–84; shipped 1885 in 214 crates
Her iron framework: Gustave Eiffel's design (UNESCO)

lines.text: By sunrise, she's wading across New York Harbor, and the whole city is filming.
I literally just bought the T-shirt!
The harbour seals dive. The gulls take off.
The Staten Island Ferry reverses, very, very carefully.
Where's she going? East. Home.

badges.text: Harbour seals and humpbacks are back in New York waters

lines.text: Paris is about five thousand eight hundred kilometres away.
Something her size would stroll at about twenty-four kilometres an hour.
That's ten days, nonstop. Statues don't need sleep.

badges.text: Our sum: an 18 m leg at a human-like pace ≈ 24 km/h → ~10 days

lines.text: Past the harbour mouth, the sea floor drops away.
The water closes over her crown, then her torch.
New York's humpback whales have been coming back in big numbers.
None of them expected this.
Day four. Three thousand eight hundred metres down. Pitch black, except for her torch.
The pressure here is nearly four hundred times what it is at the surface.
But she's hollow, and full of seawater, so it pushes back from inside just as hard.
And then, in the torchlight, a shape everyone knows.
She lowers her torch for a moment. Then she keeps walking.

badges.text: Titanic's wreck lies about 3,800 m down (NOAA)
Our sum: +1 atmosphere per 10 m → ~380 atm
Her detour to the wreck: invented for the film

lines.text: Day six. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, part of the longest mountain range on Earth.
Almost all of it is underwater.
She climbs it in the dark. On the far side, the sea floor starts rising towards Europe.

badges.text: Mid-ocean ridge: ~65,000 km, >90% under the sea (NOAA)

lines.text: Day ten. Sunrise in Normandy.
The tides at Mont-Saint-Michel are among the biggest in Europe,
up to about fourteen metres.
The salt-meadow sheep are used to water coming in fast.
They are not used to this.

badges.text: Tides here reach ~14 m: Europe's biggest on the mainland

lines.text: Paris. The Arc de Triomphe is fifty metres tall. She's forty-six.
In New York, she has a pedestal. Here, she has to stand on her toes.

badges.text: Arc de Triomphe: ~50 m. Statue, heel to torch: 46 m (NPS)

lines.text: Parisians last saw her in 1884, the colour of a new penny. She's come back green.
And her skeleton and that tower came from the same engineer. Time for a family photo.

badges.text: Bright copper in 1886; the green patina took decades (ACS)

lines.text: Except the Eiffel Tower is three hundred and thirty metres tall.
She doesn't even reach the first floor.

badges.text: Eiffel Tower: 330 m with antennas; first floor at 57 m

lines.text: And on a narrow island in the Seine, someone has been waiting.
A quarter-size copy of her, put up in 1889.
Since 1937, she has faced west, towards New York.
Eighty-nine years of looking out to sea. And today, her big sister walked out of it.

badges.text: Paris replica: 11.5 m, 1889; turned to face west in 1937

lines.text: Back in New York, the pedestal is empty.
So... do I get a refund?
She'll be back. Probably.
And she may not be the only wanderer.
Some archaeologists think Easter Island's statues were walked into place,
rocked upright with ropes.
So which landmark should walk next? Tell me in the comments.

badges.text: 'Walking' moai: a tested idea, still debated

cards.title: Which landmark walks next? Comment below.

claims.text: Statues cannot walk; the scenario is a cartoon. Dee, Tony, the crowds and the animals' reactions are fictional.
The Statue of Liberty's right heel is raised, conveying forward movement, and broken shackles and chains lie at her feet (NPS).
Heel to top of torch is 151 ft 1 in (46.05 m); heel to top of head 111 ft 1 in (33.86 m); the copper skin is 3/32 inch thick, about two pennies (NPS).

The statue was completed and assembled in Paris between 1881 and 1884, presented on 4 July 1884, then taken apart and shipped on the French Navy ship Isère, arriving in New York on 17 June 1885 in 214 crates (about 350 pieces).
Gustave Eiffel's company engineered the statue's internal iron framework (Bartholdi designed the statue).

Our calculation: humans and many animals prefer to walk at a Froude number v^2/(gL) of about 0.25. Taking her leg length as about 18 m (roughly 0.53 of her 33.86 m heel-to-head height), v = sqrt(0.25 x 9.81 x 18) = 6.6 m/s, about 24 km/h. New York to Paris is about 5,837 km great-circle, so about 245 hours, or ten days, without stopping. Water drag and the Froude rule's limits for very large walkers are ignored.
Humpback whale sightings around New York City have risen sharply since about 2011 (Gotham Whale has catalogued hundreds of individuals), and harbour seals haul out on Staten Island.
The Titanic's wreck lies about 3,800 m (12,500 ft) down, roughly 370 miles south-east of Newfoundland (NOAA figures via WorldAtlas).

Our calculation: sea pressure rises about one atmosphere per 10 m (NOAA), so about 380 atmospheres at 3,800 m. A hollow statue open to the sea would fill with water and the pressure inside would match the outside, so the thin skin would not be crushed; this is our reasoning, not a tested result.
The mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, nearly 65,000 km, and more than 90 per cent of it lies under the ocean (NOAA). The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is part of it.

The bay of Mont-Saint-Michel has a tidal range of roughly 14 m, among the largest in Europe and described by the regional tourist board as the highest in continental Europe; its salt marshes are grazed by sheep (pré-salé lamb).
The Arc de Triomphe is about 50 m (49.54 m) tall and 45 m wide; its central vault is 29.19 m high. The statue is 46 m from heel to torch.
The Eiffel Tower is about 330 m tall including antennas (since a 2022 antenna); its first floor is 57 m above the ground.
The statue's copper was bright when dedicated in 1886; the green patina formed over the following decades (by about 1910 she was part copper, part green).

The bronze replica on the Île aux Cygnes in Paris is 11.5 m tall (about a quarter scale), was given by Americans in Paris and inaugurated on 4 July 1889, and was turned to face west, towards New York, in 1937. Sources disagree on which way it faced before 1937.

Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt proposed (2011-12, with a 2025 follow-up study) that Rapa Nui's moai were 'walked' upright with ropes, rocking side to side; a replica was moved this way in tests. Other archaeologists say this does not prove it happened.
Her route past the Titanic, kneeling, waving and everything else she does are invented for the film.

titles: What If the Statue of Liberty Walked Home?
The Statue of Liberty Just Walked to Paris
She's Been Mid-Step Since 1886. Now She Walks
publishing.description: Look at the Statue of Liberty's right foot: the heel is off the ground. She's been mid-stride since 1886. So what if, one night, she finished the step and walked home to Paris? We follow her out of New York Harbor, along the floor of the Atlantic past the Titanic, over the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, ashore at Mont-Saint-Michel, past the Arc de Triomphe and up to the Eiffel Tower, built by the same engineer who built her skeleton. And on a little island in the Seine, someone has been waiting for her since 1937.
publishing.whats_real: What's real: her raised heel, her size and two-penny copper skin, her 1884 assembly in Paris and 214 crates, Eiffel's framework, New York's returning whales and seals, the Titanic's depth, the mid-ocean ridge, the tides at Mont-Saint-Michel, the heights of the Arc and the Eiffel Tower, her original copper colour and the Paris replica that faces New York are sourced below. Her walking speed (about 24 km/h, ten days) and the pressure figure are our own arithmetic and are labelled ESTIMATE on screen. Statues can't walk; Dee and Tony are fictional.
